entities.summary: Hōjō Takatoki  was the last Tokusō and ruling Shikken (regent) of Japan's Kamakura shogunate; the rulers that followed were his puppets. A member of the Hōjō clan, he was the son of Hōjō Sadatoki, and was preceded as shikken by Hōjō Mototoki.

entities.name: Hōjō Takatoki
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Hōjō Takatoki, born on January 17, 1304, served as the fourteenth and final Tokusō (head of the Hōjō clan) and Shikken (regent) of the Kamakura shogunate, a pivotal role that placed him at the apex of Japan's warrior government during a period of profound instability. Though formally the regent, he largely functioned as a puppet master, controlling a succession of nominal shikken while the true power of the shogunate eroded under the weight of internal clan disputes, economic strain, and growing provincial discontent. His reign, culminating in his death on July 12, 1333, marked the definitive end of the Hōjō clan's 150-year dominance and the collapse of Japan's first warrior government.

His effective rule, spanning from 1316 to 1333, was characterized by a perceived detachment from governance, often attributed to his reported indulgence in pastimes such as dog fighting and lavish entertainments, which alienated many provincial samurai who felt neglected and undercompensated. This perceived fecklessness exacerbated the existing financial woes of the shogunate, which struggled to reward its vassals following the Mongol invasions of the late 13th century. The emperor Go-Daigo, seizing on the shogunate's weakness and widespread dissatisfaction, launched the Genkō War in 1331, aiming to restore direct imperial rule, a movement that garnered significant support from disaffected warriors like Ashikaga Takauji and Nitta Yoshisada.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hōjō Takatoki's reign and ultimate defeat led to the collapse of the Kamakura Shogunate, ending over 150 years of Hōjō rule and initiating a major transition in Japan's political landscape from imperial restoration to the subsequent Ashikaga Shogunate.
